after: ## The role law plays in society
alt: Three views. Roscoe Pound: law as social engineering, balancing individual, public and social interests. Émile Durkheim: simple societies rely on repressive law that punishes, complex societies on restitutive law that restores, matching the growth of civil law. A Marxist critique: law protects those with economic power.
caption: Pound explains balancing, Durkheim the growth of civil law, Marx the doubts.

alt: A right becomes enforceable through a chain: an expectation is recognised in law, gives standing before a court or tribunal, and leads to a remedy. Examples: the Consumer Rights Act 2015, unfair dismissal, the Human Rights Act 1998 and negligence damages. In R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor, tribunal fees caused claims to fall sharply and the Supreme Court quashed them.
caption: Cost, delay and lack of advice can leave a right on paper only.

alt: Four pairings of competing interests: public and private (Kennaway v Thompson’s limiting injunction; Coventry v Lawrence), individual and state (police powers and safeguards under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984), individual and individual (privacy against expression in Campbell v MGN), and public policy against a claimant (Hill v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire).
caption: Almost every rule weighs one interest against another; courts often split the difference.

after: ## The meaning and importance of fault
alt: A narrowing ladder of fault: intention at the top, then subjective recklessness, negligence and finally strict liability, which needs no fault for at least one element. Fault grades the offence (murder or manslaughter) and the sentence (culpability). Alphacell v Woodward and Harrow LBC v Shah show strict liability; Sweet v Parsley shows the presumption of mens rea.
caption: The more blameworthy the mind, the more serious the offence and sentence.

after: ## The meaning and importance of fault
alt: Civil law uses objective fault in negligence (Nettleship v Weston), reduces damages for the claimant’s own fault (contributory negligence; Froom v Butcher), and imposes some liability without fault (vicarious liability, Rylands v Fletcher, Consumer Protection Act 1987). A table weighs arguments for fault-based liability against relying only on fault.
caption: Fault is the default in civil law too, but not the only basis for liability.

after: ## Worked example: an extended answer plan
alt: A six-step plan: define fault and link it to mens rea; set out the hierarchy of fault; show how it grades offences and sentences; introduce strict liability (Alphacell; Harrow v Shah); evaluate using Sweet v Parsley; and conclude that fault is central with limited, justified departures.
caption: Each step should say why fault matters, not just that it exists.
